output.headline: Jamaica secures privy council hearing date for slavery reparations case
output.standfirst: Jamaica's minister of culture says the privy council will hear the slavery reparations petition in March 2027, with the UK given until November to file its case, despite the government's insistence it will not pay.
output.bodyHtml:
A high-level United Kingdom appeals court has set a date to hear Jamaica's petition for legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations from the UK, the Jamaican government says.

Olivia Grange, Jamaica's minister of culture, says a hearing has been provisionally set for the week of 8 March 2027 by the London-based privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.

She added that the UK has until November this year to file its case.

Related: Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery

Last month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to London to file the petition with King Charles, Jamaica's head of state. It seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.

On 23 September, Grange told Jamaica's parliament that King Charles had referred the matter to the privy council, describing the referral as a 'big deal'. She said: 'The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions.'

Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833, which allows the monarch to refer questions of 'legal or constitutional nature' to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country's legal counsels.

The minister said that taking the matter to the international court of justice (ICJ) was not an option for Jamaica because the UK has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ that prevent the court from adjudicating on disputes between the UK and the government of any other country which is or has been a member of the Commonwealth.

Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham repeated the government's long-held position that 'the UK does not and will not pay reparations'.
output.progress: Jamaica has already filed its formal petition with King Charles, seeking a ruling on whether slavery was lawful and whether Britain owes restitution.

context.text: Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged action plan with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a reparations deal, regional leaders say.
